articles.headline: Letters to Slaveholders -- No. II
articles.author: ELL
articles.summary: Second in an original signed series (For the Pennsylvania Freeman) examining the basis on which the claim to the persons of slaves is founded. The writer, signing 'ELL', argues that the slaveholder's title traces back to the African slave trade -- pronounced piracy and punishable by death under the acts of Congress from 1807 to 1820 -- and that a title founded on an act of piracy is worthless; that a person born into slavery in America is still unjustly deprived of an inalienable right; and that until the negro's right to his own mental and physical powers has passed from him by his own act, that right cannot vest in another.

articles.headline: Slavery in the Church -- New School General Assembly
articles.summary: Report of the debate on slavery at the New School Presbyterian General Assembly. Memorials from several presbyteries asking action were referred to a committee; the report affirming the 1818 act (declaring slavery inconsistent with the law of God) was opposed by Southern delegates (Dr. Hill of the District of Columbia, formerly of Winchester, Va.; John J. Royall of Winchester). Dr. Cox of New York moved to strike the reference to the 1818 act; Alvan Stewart and John Rankin of Ohio spoke forcefully for the abolition side; F. W. Graves of Alton and George Beecher of Rochester figured in the amendments. The Assembly finally referred the subject of slavery to the synods, presbyteries and six hundred churches to 'remove the evil' -- which the Freeman judged a step in advance of previous action.

events.name: Pennsylvania State Anti-Slavery Society (Eastern District) -- Sixth Annual Meeting
events.location: Baptist meeting house, borough of Norristown, Pennsylvania
events.description: Sixth annual meeting of the Pennsylvania State Anti-Slavery Society for the Eastern District, held at Norristown on May 20, 21 and 22, 1839. Vice-President Nathan Stem took the chair; Daniel Neall Jr. and James Fulton Jr. served as assistant secretaries. The Executive Committee reported on the past six months (recovery of damages for the burning of Pennsylvania Hall; agents C. C. Burleigh, Wm. M. Chase and James Fulton Jr.; German-language work by editor C. F. Stollmeyer; the Montrose convention of ~400; auxiliary and Philadelphia society activity, including schools and house-to-house work among the colored population), and Treasurer James Wood presented his account. The society adopted a new constitution reorganizing itself as the 'Anti-Slavery Society of Eastern Pennsylvania' and elected new officers. Guest speakers from New York -- Gerrit Smith, Henry B. Stanton and James C. Fuller -- addressed the meeting. A long roll of delegates by county and local society was adopted (matched automatically from the body text).
